university: Hamburg University of Technology (Technische Universitat Hamburg, TUHH)
competition_series: FSG (Formula Student Germany), FS East, FS Czech
summary: e-gnition Hamburg, founded in 2011, converted its existing electric car (egn16, 'Uwe') into a driverless entry (egn_dv17) in nine months during 2017, one year ahead of when FSG required driverless integration - making it one of the earliest driverless conversions among German teams. That first-year effort won the Autonomous Design award and placed 3rd overall in the Driverless class at FSG 2017, an unusually strong debut. The team ran DV and EV as separate cars through 2019 before merging them into a single combined DV/EV platform for egn20 in 2020, with steering actuation integrated into a quick-release steering wheel to allow fast switching between modes. e-gnition also founded and hosts the Autonomous Racing Workshop (ARWo), an annual cross-team FS driverless conference at TUHH, reflecting a strong public/community documentation culture. Results have been volatile since (from 2nd at FS East 2023 to 25th at FSG 2024), consistent with the chronic FS problem of year-over-year knowledge loss on a large (>80-student) all-volunteer team.

ramp_phases: Named/inferable phases from team history: (1) 'egn_dv17' - fast 9-month conversion of an existing EV chassis into a standalone DV car (2017); (2) separate-car era - DV and EV run as distinct vehicles with growing sensor counts (2017-2019); (3) 'egn20' combined-platform era - single chassis switchable between EV and DV via quick-release steering wheel/front wing (2020-present).
what_slipped: [uncertain] No explicit team statement of schedule slips found in sources reviewed. Strong indirect evidence of season-to-season inconsistency: results swing dramatically year to year on the same combined platform (e.g. FS East 2023: 2nd / FSG 2023: 15th in the same season; FSG 2024 dropped to 25th, the lowest recorded result, before recovering to 1st at FSG 2026). This pattern - a large, all-volunteer team producing wildly different flagship-event outcomes across seasons - is consistent with, though not confirmed as caused by, turnover-driven knowledge loss on a >80-member team rather than a single named component slip.
platform_prerequisites: Yes initially - egn_dv17 (2017) was a driverless conversion of an already-existing EV chassis (egn16), completed in 9 months, so no new EV platform had to be built first. From 2020 onward (egn20) the team went further and unified DV and EV into one physical platform switchable via a quick-release steering wheel and front wing, eliminating the need to build/maintain two separate chassis.
ebs_design: [uncertain] Specific EBS architecture (pneumatic/hydraulic accumulator, actuator model, deceleration figures) not found in sources reviewed for e-gnition specifically. General FSAE/FSG DT.3.2 requirement applies (passive mechanically-stored-energy system, <=200ms reaction time, >10 m/s^2 average deceleration, half performance on single failure) but no team-specific implementation detail was sourced.
steering_actuation: Steering actuation is fully integrated into the steering wheel assembly itself (rather than mounted separately on the rack/column) and is designed to be easily exchangeable via a quick-release mechanism, allowing the same egn20 chassis to switch between manual EV steering wheel and DV steering-actuator wheel (along with a front-wing swap) between EV and DV configurations. Specific actuator model, motor sizing, or DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism detail was not found in sources reviewed. [uncertain: decoupling implementation detail]

chassis_impact: Chassis strategy evolved from full-car conversion (2017: driverless hardware retrofitted onto the existing egn16 EV chassis) to a purpose-built combined DV/EV chassis (egn20, 2020) engineered from the outset for quick-swap between EV and DV configurations via steering wheel and front wing changes - a more significant chassis/interface design commitment than a pure retrofit.

No secondary dedicated safety MCU beyond the LPC4337 was identified in sources reviewed. [uncertain: exact current-generation (2022+) compute platform not found]

IMU/GNSS/wheel-speed/steering-encoder models not found in sources reviewed. [uncertain: exact current (2022+) sensor suite]

critical_path_items: 1) Converting the prior year's electric-only chassis (egn16) into a driverless-capable car within a single 9-month season while retaining that car's electric-class competitiveness; 2) building a from-scratch autonomous track-recognition software stack with an interdisciplinary, largely first-time team; 3) later, engineering a single chassis (egn20) that could reliably switch between EV and DV configurations via a quick-release steering wheel and front wing without compromising either mode's tech-inspection compliance.

recommended_sequence: Synthesized from e-gnition's history (not an explicit team statement): 1) If an EV platform already exists, prioritize a fast (single-season, ~9-month) conversion over a from-scratch DV chassis - e-gnition proved this can still produce a podium-caliber Driverless-class result in the very first attempt. 2) Start driverless work ahead of any external deadline/mandate rather than at the last responsible moment, as the team explicitly chose to do relative to FSG's rollout schedule. 3) Grow sensor count/coverage incrementally after the first working system (1 camera/2 LiDAR in year one, expanding to 2 cameras/5 LiDAR by year three) rather than over-speccing the sensor suite before the software stack can use it. 4) Only invest in unifying EV and DV into a single switchable chassis (as with egn20) once the separate-car approach has matured and proven the DV subsystems independently - this is a second-generation optimization, not a starting point. 5) Institutionalize cross-team knowledge sharing early (e-gnition's ARWo workshop is a team-level mechanism for this, but internal onboarding appears to remain a persistent weak point based on results volatility) - UMSAE should build internal documentation discipline from day one rather than relying solely on external community engagement.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Highly applicable for the 'how fast can a conversion go' question: e-gnition's 9-month, single-season conversion of an existing EV chassis into a podium-finishing driverless car (3rd place, FSG 2017, on debut) is strong evidence that UMSAE's 24-month window (June 2026 to June 2028) is generous by comparison, provided the platform-reuse strategy is followed. However, e-gnition's subsequent decade of highly volatile results (from 1st to 25th place across seasons on the same class of platform) is an important cautionary signal for UMSAE: a fast first-year ramp does not by itself guarantee sustained performance, and UMSAE - with a fixed, small (~9-person) software-focused team rather than e-gnition's 80+-member all-volunteer pool - should weight process/documentation discipline and knowledge retention more heavily than raw first-year speed, since it cannot rely on e-gnition's scale to absorb turnover losses each season.
